file_lines.section: 2.4 Faces already woven, but without the *why*
file_lines.text: | God's inner speech about the evil inclination | grief and judgement (Gen 6:5–7) · forbearance (Gen 8:21) | 11 §8, 12 |

- **The Hebrew Bible:** The source is the *lēv* (heart), not the brain. Examples are Proverbs 4:23 ("from it flow the springs of life") and Genesis 6:5 ("every intention of the thoughts of his heart").
- Genesis 6:5 speaks of "the intention of the thoughts of his heart," and Luke 1:51 of "the thoughts of their hearts."

5. **Transient, yet weighty.** Human thoughts are "but a breath" (Psalm 94:11) and "futile" (1 Corinthians 3:20). Yet God weighs them (Proverbs 15:26), and before the flood they were the measure of human wickedness (Genesis 6:5). God's thoughts, by contrast, are "very deep" (Psalm 92:5), "vast" (Psalm 139:17) and "higher" (Isaiah 55:8–9).
| intention / intent | H3336 *yēṣer* | Gen 8:21 | *yēṣer* is also in Gen 6:5; central to origins |

The *arising* is not commanded, but it is not neutral either. What comes up shows the condition of the heart (Gen 6:5; Mark 7:21). So thoughts that arise reveal the heart, and devising engages the will. The heart itself can be changed from outside: written on, given discretion, guarded, or darkened.

the origin-of-thought words in M64 (H2803G, H2803H, H2803I chashab (devise, plan) 73 hits; H3336 yetser (frame, purpose) 5 hits), each hit with no face: how each names where thought starts, and what it moves, in its own verses

file_lines.text: 1. **Design: forming something that does not yet exist.** H2803G (19 rows) describes craftsmanship: cherubim "skillfully worked" (Exod 26:1, 31) and "skilled design" (Exod 39:3). The faculty itself is neutral. *Maḥăšāvāh* covers both artistry and plots, and *mᵊzimmāh* covers both "discretion" (Prov 2:11) and "evil devices" (Prov 12:2). What makes a thought good or evil is **what it is designed toward**.

file_lines.text: | **Craft and design** | Exo 31:4; 35:32–35; 2Ch 2:14; 26:15 ("invented by skillful men") |

This refines the earlier point. The *capacity* to devise isn't good or evil in itself; it's what artisans and God also do. Thought, on this evidence, means **designing a form that doesn't exist yet**, and what makes a thought good or evil is **what it is designed toward**. It also bears on where thought comes from: Exodus 35:35 says of the craftsmen, "He has **filled them** with skill," so their ability to design is described as given to them.

Numbers 17:5: "Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel"
file_lines.text: The verse closes a long dispute over who God has chosen. It begins in Numbers 16. Korah and 250 chiefs, *"chosen from the assembly, well-known men"* (16:2; *qārîʾ*, H7148, "called"), rise up: *"Why then do you exalt yourselves above the assembly of the Lord?"* (16:3). Moses answers with God's choosing: *"The one whom he chooses he will bring near to him"* (16:5), and *"the man whom the Lord chooses shall be the holy one"* (16:7).
- God making himself known, an operation: Num 16:5, Eze 20:5

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

**Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also?"* (Num 16:10). The grumbling at Aaron was against God: *"What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (16:11), and God calls it *"the grumblings … which they grumble against you"*, to be made to *"cease from me"* (17:5). Psalm 106 names the inner act: *"men in the camp were jealous of Moses and Aaron"* (Psa 106:16). God's reply was to make the choice plain, with the staff that sprouted. Then the grumbling became terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (Num 17:13).

verses.text: But you shall seek the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there. There you shall go,

observations.text: Deut.12.5 'seek the place' draws on the 'resort to, frequent' sense (1a1) combined with devotional pursuit of the divinely chosen worship-site; a standard extension within the base gloss, no notable divergence.

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: The phrase is a weighty one in Deuteronomy. *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same shape as the phrase Deuteronomy uses for the Lord’s own choosing: *"the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes"* (12:5); *"the place that the Lord will choose in one of your tribes"* (12:14). The words (place, that, choose, in one of your …) are the same (H4725, H0977). I read this as the law giving the escaped slave, in his own small measure, the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw the comparison.
The same verb is used of the Lord choosing the place for his name (Deu 12:5, 14), and of the Lord's answering choice: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (Isa 66:4).

The phrase *"the place that he shall choose within one of your towns"* has the same wording as *"the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (Deu 12:5, 14). I read this as the law giving the slave a small share of the kind of choosing the Lord keeps for his own dwelling. The verse does not draw this comparison (open item).

file_lines.text: - Willing: pressing (Judg 19:7–9; 2Sa 13:25–27), enticing (Deu 13:6–8; Pro 1:10), the crowd (Mar 15:15), friends restraining or encouraging (Act 19:30–31; 18:27), objection (Act 28:19), consent sought so that the good is free (Phm 14).

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": §2c batch 1, others around the choosing: the place God chooses (Deu 12:18, Deu 12:21, Deu 14:23, Deu 16:11, Deu 16:15, Deu 17:10, Deu 18:6, 1Ki 8:48, 2Ch 6:38, Neh 1:9)
Deuteronomy 18:6: "and he may come when he desires"
file_lines.text: Two choosings stand in the passage. file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 16:11 and 16:15: "you shall rejoice before the Lord your God" and "you will be altogether joyful"
file_lines.text: **The Feast of Weeks** is a feast of rejoicing: *"And you shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your towns, the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place that the Lord your God will choose"* (v11). file_lines.section: 3.1 God chooses: a place, so that his name dwells there (44)
file_lines.text: - judgement: Deu 17:8, 17:10

**Carefulness, against presumption.** When a case is *"too difficult for you"* (17:8), the decision is sought at the place. What is asked of the person then is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:10), and not to turn *"to the right hand or to the left"* (17:11). Presumption is the opposite, and the man who acts presumptuously dies. The end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage gives the limit (*"too difficult for you"*) and the carefulness. It does not describe the inner struggle.

file_lines.section: 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live
file_lines.text: ### 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live

file_lines.section: 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live
file_lines.text: - **Choice:** the slave's: *"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"* (v16).

file_lines.section: 6. Deu 23:16 — the escaped slave chooses where to live
file_lines.text: - **Outcome:** Given as law, not narrated: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst … You shall not wrong him"* (v16). Israel is to honour the choice and not hand him back: *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15).

- **The held phrasing in 10.7.** The working note in 10.7 holds the shared phrasing of Deuteronomy 23:16 (*"in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him"*) and Deuteronomy 12:5, 14. Batch 1 read Deuteronomy 12 in full. The forms of words differ: 12:5 has *"out of all your tribes"*, 12:14 *"in one of your tribes"*, and 23:16 *"within one of your towns"*. In 23:16 the chooser is the escaped slave. The reading does not settle whether the shared phrase is more than a form of words. It stays held.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: **For the next batches:** batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: ## Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"

file_lines.section: Deuteronomy 23:16 — "in the place that he shall choose … wherever it suits him"
file_lines.text: The law concerns *"a slave who has escaped from his master to you"*. Israel is told *"You shall not give up to his master"* (v15). Then the choice is handed to the slave: *"He shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (v16).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - Deu 23:16 echoes the phrase used for the place the Lord chooses (Deu 12). I have marked this "I read". Whether it is to be read as more than a shared form of words is for the researcher.
- **The escaped slave:** "in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him" (Deu 23:16).

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16

**What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).

- **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.
- **Deu 23:16 and Deu 12.** Whether the shared phrase is more than a shared form of words (marked "I read").
| Deu 23:16 | rests on the chooser's own good; a choice that is honoured; faces (a place) | batch 3 |
- **The held phrase** (Deu 23:16 beside Deu 12:5, 14) stays held. The forms of words differ (*"out of all your tribes"*, *"in one of your tribes"*, *"within one of your towns"*).

file_lines.section: 1. The faces of the word (#1919, Ch 11 §4)
file_lines.text: | Wishing | Job 9:3; 13:3; 33:32; Deu 25:7–8 | to contend with God; to justify another; not wanting a duty |

- **Not wanting a duty:** "if the man does not wish to take his brother's wife … if he persists, saying, I do not wish to take her" (Deu 25:7–8). Then the gate, the sandal, the spit, and the name "The house of him who had his sandal pulled off" (25:9–10). The law does not force the wanting. It makes the not-wanting public and gives it a name.

observations.text: jealousy is named beside the anger in the setting of other gods and broken covenant.
both verses put the heart first and the anger after it. In Deuteronomy the verb is "smoke" (ʿāšan).

ʿāšan is the word for Sinai smoking when God came down, and for mountains smoking at his touch. In Psa 74:1 and Deu 29:20 it is the word for his anger toward his people. In Psa 80:4 the ESV renders it "be angry", and it is against "your people's prayers".

file_lines.section: 1.6 *Ashan* H6225 "smoke" (6 verses), *meribah* H4809H / H4808, and the remaining single-verse words
file_lines.text: - ***Ashan*.** The anger word is **literally smoke**: Sinai "wrapped in smoke" (Exo 19:18), and mountains that "smoke" at his touch (Psa 104:32; 144:5). Where it is anger, it is **divine anger answering a human heart**. In Deu 29:20, "the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will smoke against that man". The man is described in 29:18–19: one "whose heart is turning away … blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'". **The seat in the passage is the human's secret self-blessing, and the anger answers it.**

file_lines.text: ### 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve

file_lines.section: 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve
file_lines.text: - **Led to:** Joshua recounts what the Lord gave: *"a land on which you had not labored"* (v13). Then he calls on them: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods"* (v14). The choice is put to them on one condition: *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day whom you will serve"* (v15).

file_lines.section: 1. Jos 24:15 — Israel at Shechem chooses whom to serve
file_lines.text: - Joshua chooses first: *"as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord"* (v15).
- Jos 24:15 and 22 (*"choose this day whom you will serve"*) make serving **what is chosen**. It is still counted as an operation.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [the test](m64-choose-test-reading-v1-20261007.md): Jos 24:15, Psa 119:30, Isa 65:12
- **The chooser's eyes.** *"if it is evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, choose this day"* (Jos 24:15). Here the chooser's own sight is where turning from the Lord could begin.
- It is the chooser's sight, from which turning from the Lord could begin (Jos 24:15).

- **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: 1.2 What the "no" protects, and what it costs
file_lines.text: - Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1Sa 15:9). The refusal was selective. They destroyed what they did not value and kept what they did. God's word follows: *"he has turned back from following me"* (15:11), and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 2](m64-choose-2c-reading-batch2-others-ot-v1-20261008.md), other Old Testament: Num 17:5, Judg 20:34, 1Sa 20:30, 2Sa 6:16, Psa 106:5, Psa 106:23, Pro 10:20, Isa 7:16, Isa 45:4, Isa 49:7, Isa 58:5, Isa 66:3, Jer 33:24

**Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul to Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1Sa 20:30). Saul calls the choice shame and gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). His anger is for his house. It goes from insult to a death sentence to a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan's choice was made in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His own anger answers his father's, and it is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). The choice holds, sealed by an oath *"in the name of the Lord"* (20:42).

observations.text: In 1 Sam 24.2 and 26.2, 'seek' carries a hostile-pursuit nuance (seeking to kill/capture David) rather than the neutral/benign 'seek to find' sense; this militarised sense diverges from the more affectionate or petitionary uses elsewhere (e.g. Song 3.1, Exod 10.11), showing the verb's flexibility to carry either amicable or adversarial intent depending on context.
Saul (party) initiates the seek-operation, directed toward David and his men (party), moving into the wilderness terrain to locate them -- a hostile pursuit operation.

M64 (chosen, of the men) is present but concerns selection/election rather than seeking; seeking here targets a person (David) not a quality, so no direct conceptual overlap with the co-present M-code.

file_lines.section: What the chosen are moved to
file_lines.text: - **Celebrating.** *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21). The celebrating had stopped at Uzzah's death, when David was angry, afraid and unwilling (6:8–10). It came back when he heard of the Lord's blessing (6:12).

The chosen live before God's sight, not others'. David answers Michal, who measured him by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20): *"It was before the Lord, who chose me"*, and *"I will be abased in your eyes"* (6:21–22). The purpose of the choosing in Ephesians is to be holy and blameless *"before him"* (Eph 1:4).

**Before whom.** David celebrates *"before the Lord"* against Michal's measure of the servants' eyes (2Sa 6:20–22). This sits with §2a, "whose measure": the eyes that judge the choice.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": §2c batch 2, others around the choosing, Old Testament (Num 17:5, Judg 20:34, 1Sa 20:30, 2Sa 6:16, Psa 106:5, Psa 106:23, Pro 10:20, Isa 7:16, Isa 45:4, Isa 49:7, Isa 58:5, Isa 66:3, Jer 33:24)
file_lines.text: - 2 Samuel 6:1–23 (read for §2b; read again here for Michal)

**Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

file_lines.section: 3.5 God chooses a person for a task or office (40)
file_lines.text: - David: "who chose me above your father … to appoint me as prince over Israel, the people of the Lord —and I will celebrate before the Lord" (2Sa 6:21)

**Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2Sa 6:16). The contempt is inward before it is spoken. When it comes out, its measure is honour before others: *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (6:20). David answers by naming the choosing: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father"* (6:21).

**Whose eyes.** In four of these the measure is named, and it is set against God's: *"in his own eyes"* against the place God chooses (Deu 12:8); *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:20–21); *"in their sight"* (Jer 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4).

| **One further citation fix found** | 1 | 2Sa 14:13–14 in 10.7 *Planning* (§3.12) |

**2Sa 14:13–14, in 10.7 *Planning*.** This is a citation fix of the #1990 kind: the same Joab issue in a place the #1987 reading did not list. Replace the paragraph that begins *"A plan can also be held against someone's good"* with:

> A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).

### 2. 2Sa 19:38 — Barzillai's choice for Chimham

- **Choice:** The king hands the choice to Barzillai: *"I will do for him whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (v38). The choice made is Barzillai's: Chimham goes in his place.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: **For the next batches:** batch 3 is people choosing of their own accord, and choosing together (Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25), with the wisdom sayings Pro 3:31 and 16:16. These are mostly not choices between God and other gods. Whether they show the same tie to what the eyes see, to delight and to knowing is to be read from them.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 3 — choosing of one's own accord, choosing together, and the wisdom sayings
2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"
file_lines.text: ## 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as a person's own freedom, honoured.** In Deu 23:16 and 2Sa 19:38 the ground is the chooser's own good: *"wherever it suits him"*, *"whatever seems good to you"*. Others are bound to honour it. This is a face not seen in batches 1–2, where the choosing was between the Lord and something else. Here "good in your eyes" is honoured. In Jos 24:15, "evil in your eyes" was where the choice against the Lord could start. The same expression changes character with the setting (#1919).
- "all that you desire of me I will do for you" (2Sa 19:38)

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16
- *"desire"*: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38)

**What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deu 23:16) and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2Sa 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.

Yet "good in your eyes" is not always the wrong measure. When the king says *"whatever seems good to you"* to the old man who served him (2Sa 19:38), the chooser's own eyes are honoured. The setting changes what the same expression means. (See "What changes the character" below.)

Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and Scripture gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you … in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deu 23:16). The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2Sa 19:38).
- It is the chooser's own good, honoured by the king (2Sa 19:38).

file_lines.section: 3. The Hebrew: the will is the yes or no to another
file_lines.text: - **Something offered at a cost to others:** David *"would not drink it"* and gives his reason: *"Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?"* (2Sa 23:16–17).

file_lines.section: 1.1 The will meets something put before it
file_lines.text: - **A gift:** water from Bethlehem, brought at the risk of three men's lives (2Sa 23:16–17; 1Ch 11:18–19).

file_lines.section: 1.2 What the "no" protects, and what it costs
file_lines.text: - David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water'"* (2Sa 23:15). When it came, *"he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for the sake of the men's lives. He gave the reason aloud, before the Lord.

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **Wanting and refusing.** David's longing for the water, then his refusal for the men's sake (2Sa 23:15–17). For 10.6 *Wanting*, beside choosing.

file_lines.section: 3. The Hebrew: the will is the yes or no to another
file_lines.text: - **Something offered at a cost to others:** David *"would not drink it"* and gives his reason: *"Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?"* (2Sa 23:16–17).

file_lines.section: 1.1 The will meets something put before it
file_lines.text: - **A gift:** water from Bethlehem, brought at the risk of three men's lives (2Sa 23:16–17; 1Ch 11:18–19).

file_lines.section: 1.2 What the "no" protects, and what it costs
file_lines.text: - David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water'"* (2Sa 23:15). When it came, *"he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for the sake of the men's lives. He gave the reason aloud, before the Lord.

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **Wanting and refusing.** David's longing for the water, then his refusal for the men's sake (2Sa 23:15–17). For 10.6 *Wanting*, beside choosing.

| *ʾāḇâ* | refusing God (Isa 30:15); refusing sin (Pro 1:10); refusing to harm the anointed (1Sa 26:23); refusing a gift for others' sake (2Sa 23:17); refusing a plea by force (2Sa 13:14); refusing in grief (2Sa 12:17); God not willing to destroy (2Ki 8:19); God not willing to forgive (Deu 29:20) | What is refused, and for whose sake. The passages give the reason each time: faith, fear, grief, honour, force, covenant, love, a stubborn heart |

verses.text: “And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought. If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.

observations.text: In Isa.58.2, Ezra.6.21, and 1Chr.28.9 'seek/worship' sits squarely within the base cultic-consultation/devotion sense of H1875, with no further distinguishing nuance beyond ordinary devotional seeking of God.

M15 (know), M36 (serve), M34 (whole/forever), M47 (heart/mind), M64 (plan), M06 (thought), M30/M59 (forsake), M18 (willing) all co-occur with H1875 in 1Chr.28.9; H1875's own vantage is that the verse pairs two mirrored uses of darash -- human seeking of God and divine searching of the heart -- forming the verse's relational spine that the other M-codes (serving, willing heart, forsaking) orbit as conditions or consequences of that mutual seeking.

1Chr.28.9, Prov.11.27, and Job.39.8 all render darash as 'searches' but span three distinct registers: God searching all hearts (devotional-omniscient), a person searching for evil (moral-negative object), and a wild animal searching for pasture (literal/animal). This triad illustrates the verb's semantic elasticity across divine, moral, and mundane subjects within one surface form.

God's extension of the characteristic (his willingness to be sought/found) is shown as both conditional and responsive: conditional on genuine seeking ('If you seek him, he will be found by you, but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever', 1Chr.28.9), yet also shown as gracious and unconditioned in Isa.65.1 ('I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me') -- God's self-disclosure as available to be inquired of exceeds strict conditionality, showing both a covenantal-conditional pattern and a gracious-responsive pattern.

Adjacent characteristics appearing alongside seeking include 'heart/mind' (M47, frequently paired as the seat/manner of seeking, e.g. 1Chr.22.19, 2Chr.15.12, Ps.119.2/10), 'trust' (M19, Ps.9.10, Isa.31.1), and 'forsake' (M30/M59, as antithetical pairing, Ps.9.10, 1Chr.28.9) -- these co-occur with notable frequency, showing seeking is characteristically bound to heart-language and its antithesis, forsaking.

Seeking consistently PRECEDES finding/being found and its resulting blessings: Jer.29.13 'You will seek me and find me'; Isa.55.6 'Seek the Lord while he may be found'; 1Chr.28.9 'If you seek him, he will be found by you' -- the sequence is invariably seek-then-find, never the reverse, establishing seeking as the necessary antecedent condition.

The seek-then-find sequence is causal-conditional rather than merely correlational or developmental: the finding is explicitly conditioned upon the seeking ('IF you seek him, he WILL be found'), establishing a covenantal cause-and-effect relationship rather than a coincidental temporal succession.
yēṣer ("intention", "inclination") is the same word as the potter's thing formed, and as our frame. The inclination of the heart is itself something formed
God knows the inclination before it acts ("what they are inclined to do even today")
Thoughts are fully open to God and to Jesus. Jesus perceives inner questioning "in his spirit"

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **Knowing is not enough.** Belshazzar *"knew all this"* and did not humble his heart (Dan 5:22). In the plan set, God *"understands every plan"* (1Ch 28:9). The will set adds that the person's own knowing does not move the will.

verses.text: Then Hezekiah said, “You have now consecrated yourselves to the Lord. Come near; bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the Lord.” And the assembly brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings.

observations.text: In 2Chr 29:31 and 2Chr 33:16 'thank offerings'/'thanksgiving' sit squarely within todah's cultic-sacrificial base gloss with no notable shift.

In 2Chr 29:31, todah (thank offerings) co-occurs with M22 (glory-related 'said'), M23/M72 (consecrated), M44 (assembly), M09/M34 (willing), M47 (heart), M36 (burnt offerings). Todah's own contribution: it names the specific sacrificial category the consecrated assembly brings, standing alongside but distinct from the burnt offerings (M36) which serve full dedication rather than gratitude.

In 2Chr 29:31 the operation-words 'bring'/'brought' (H0935P, role-T3) are initiated by Hezekiah's assembly, directed toward the house of the Lord, carrying todah offerings as the object of the action.

Across its full occurrence list H8426 clusters into three recurring realizations of one lexeme: (1) the concrete thank-offering sacrifice (Lev.7.12 x2, Lev.7.13, Lev.7.15, Lev.22.29, Ps.50.14, Ps.50.23, Ps.107.22, Ps.116.17, Amos.4.5, Jonah.2.9, 2Chr.29.31 x2, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11), (2) the vocal/manner accompaniment of praise, 'with/in thanksgiving' (Ps.69.30, Ps.26.7, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Isa.51.3), and (3) the institutional thanksgiving choir/procession/company (Neh.12.27, Neh.12.31, Neh.12.38, Neh.12.40, Ps.42.4). A fourth, rarer sense realizes it as verbal confession (Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11). This is a single strong showing internally the full sense-range attributed to the subgroup label (hymn, choir, offering) without needing a second member strong to supply any of these senses.

Since H8426 is the sole member strong of this subgroup, there is no second lexeme to compare it against directly; the meaningful cross-comparison available is internal -- between H8426's own sacrificial/cultic-object occurrences (e.g. Lev.7.12-15, Lev.22.29, 2Chr.29.31, 2Chr.33.16, Jer.17.26, Jer.33.11, Amos.4.5) versus its choir/procession-as-institution occurrences (Neh.12.27-40, Ps.42.4) versus its purely adverbial/manner occurrences ('with thanksgiving', e.g. Ps.69.30, Ps.95.2, Ps.100.4, Ps.147.7, Ps.26.7). These three groupings do not overlap grammatically: the sacrificial sense is always the head noun or a construct-genitive qualifier of an offering-word (zebach, shelamim), the choir sense functions as a collective-body noun (subject or object of appointment/movement verbs), and the manner sense is marked by a preposition (b-) modifying a separate main verb of praise. No morphological distinction (all occurrences are the same feminine noun stem, singular or plural absolute/construct) drives this three-way split -- it is purely syntactic/contextual, meaning the noun's referent is disambiguated entirely by its syntactic role in each verse rather than by any inflectional change.

Todah takes hold rightly under conditions of a willing heart (2Chr.29.31, 'all who were of a willing heart') and right ordering of one's way of life (Ps.50.23, 'to one who orders his way rightly'); it operates rightly when accompanied by genuine acknowledgment rather than mere ritual performance.

The human-to-God movement of todah requires an inner posture of humility and right-ordering ('to one who orders his way rightly,' Ps.50.23), willingness ('willing heart,' 2Chr.29.31), and honest acknowledgment (confession, Josh.7.19, Ezra.10.11) rather than mere external ritual performance.

2Chr.29.31 shows that genuine extension of todah is accompanied by consecration ('you have now consecrated yourselves to the Lord') and a willing heart, indicating that inner conditions of dedication and voluntary devotion in the giver (here, the assembly/nation) accompany the sincere bringing of thank-offerings.

2Chr.29.31 shows the assembly had first to consecrate themselves before bringing thank offerings, indicating a person must have first undergone consecration/dedication to the Lord before rightly extending todah.

Todah ends where a different sacrificial category begins: it is explicitly distinguished from the burnt offering (2Chr.29.31, 'brought sacrifices and thank offerings...brought burnt offerings') and from the peace offering more generally, being a specific sub-type marked by gratitude/acknowledgment rather than full dedication (burnt offering) or general fellowship (peace offering).

observations.text: Flow 5: what is devised comes back. The plan returns on the deviser's head (Est 9:25); the schemer is caught in his own scheme (Psa 10:2); disaster is "the fruit of their devices" (Jer 6:19). God answers "devise wickedness" with "I am devising disaster" (Mic 2:1, 3). It also comes back for good: "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Pro 21:5); "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3)

file_lines.section: 1. Wanting life itself, and wanting to "see good"
file_lines.text: **What lies behind it: the same phrase, lost.** Job uses the same words for the opposite state: *"Remember that my life is a breath; my eye will never again see good"* (Job 7:7, in Ch 2). The psalm's "desires life … that he may see good" and Job's "never again see good" are one phrase. **I read** that the want for life is a want to see good. Where the hope of seeing good is gone, life itself is weighed as a breath, and then loathed (Job 7:15–16, in Ch 2). The verses do not say this is a sequence. They use the one phrase for both states.

file_lines.text: Job speaks *"in the anguish of my spirit … in the bitterness of my soul"* (v11). file_lines.text: His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.

file_lines.section: 3. The Hebrew: the will is the yes or no to another
file_lines.text: *ʾāḇâ* (H0014) has 52 verses. **50 of them are negated**: "would not", "not willing", "unwilling", "refuse", "would have none". The other two are a question that expects "no" (*"Is the wild ox willing to serve you?"*, Job 39:9) and a condition (*"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*, Isa 1:19).

2. **Route them under rule 72.** By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).
**Nature (13.4):** *"Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?"* (Job 39:9), among the creatures God sets beyond a man's control.

file_lines.text: - The person's fear: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12).

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: Then comes the verse: *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (v12). The word "instruct" is the same in v8 and v12 (H3384B). The person who chooses here does not make up the way. The way to choose is taught, and the one who is taught it is the one who fears the Lord. The fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice. The verse does not say the man chooses well on his own; it says the Lord instructs him in what he should choose.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The way to choose is taught (Psa 25:8, 12).** The Lord instructs sinners and the humble out of his goodness, and the one who fears him is taught *"the way that he should choose"*. This stands beside Psalm 119:29, where the psalmist asks God to put the false way far off. In both psalms the chooser does not stand alone.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Fear of the Lord comes before the choosing (Psa 25:12, 14).** The test reading of Joshua 24 had *"fear the Lord and serve him"* (v14) before the choice. Psalm 25 puts the fear first explicitly: it is the man who fears whom the Lord instructs.

file_lines.section: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction"
file_lines.text: He ends by pointing to God: *"who is a teacher like him?"* (v22). "Teacher" here is H4175, from the same root as *"instruct"* in Psalm 25:8, 12 (H3384).

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 2](m64-choose-reading-batch2-psalm-promise-v1-20261007.md): Psa 25:12, Isa 56:4

**Being taught.** *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (Psa 25:12). The teaching comes from who the Lord is: *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (25:8). The psalmist asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4). In Psalm 119 he asks *"graciously teach me your law"*, and asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).

**The fear of the Lord.** In Psalm 25 the fear comes first, then the teaching, then the choice (25:12). Joshua puts the same order before the people: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness"* (Jos 24:14), and then *"choose this day"*.

verses.text: For I hear the whispering of many — terror on every side!— as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life.

observations.text: Meaning: the prophet's word is spoken as a name over a man ("a terror to yourself"). The same words are then whispered by his close friends against him. Implies: in both Jer 20 and Psa 31, the one who hears the whisper answers by turning to the Lord ("But the Lord is with me"; "But I trust in you"). The verses state both answers. In Lamentations it is God who summoned the terrors.

observations.text: In Esth.6.2, Job.10.6, Ps.24.6, Ps.27.4, Ps.34.14, Ps.35.4, and Ps.37.36 baqash is used in its standard senses (hostile pursuit, investigative search, devotional seeking, seeking peace) with no notable divergence from the base gloss.

Other M-codes present in Ps.35.4: M07 (put to shame/dishonor/disappointed), M47 (life), M15/M64 (devise). Baqash (seek after my life) names the hostile pursuit that the psalmist prays will be met with shame (M07); it is the initiating act to which the shame-outcome responds, but does not modify the shame-terms themselves.
In Ps.35.4, H1245 (seek) is an operation initiated by the psalmist's enemies, directed toward the psalmist's life ('my life') as the target — hostile pursuit.

file_lines.section: 3B.1 Poor and needy have more than one dimension (researcher's observation, 2026-10-15)
file_lines.text: **Note for reading.** In Psa 40:17, 70:5, 86:1 and 109:22, "poor" in "poor and needy" is H6041 *ʿānî*, which is tagged M24 (§5), and "needy" is H0034 (M09). This was checked in `verse_lexical`. These verses therefore sit on both sides of the M09 / M24 line.

| 3. Needy as an expression to get sympathy or help | **Not in these 27, from the poor themselves.** No poor person here speaks. Lazarus "desired to be fed" but says nothing. What appears is another face: **others speak of the poor**, and in John the words of care are a pretext (Joh 12:6). Whether "needy" said by the needy is aimed at help is a matter for the "I am poor and needy" Psalms (Psa 86:1, 70:5, 40:17, 109:22) and Pro 18:23 *"The poor use entreaties"*. |

"Let them be put to shame and dishonor who seek after my life! … Rescue me from their destruction, my precious life from the lions! … Awake and rouse yourself for my vindication" (Psa 35:4, 17, 23). "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered. Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! (Psa 80:2, 18). | **Counted:** of the five psalms in which a person calls God to "awake" with this word (Psa 7; 35; 44; 59; 80), **all five** carry life, by context: four have the speaker's life sought or taken, and Psa 80 ends "give us life". **Meaning:** the call to God to wake rises where life is under threat. **Implies (R):** I read the cry as speaking from how it feels when God does not act: "Why are you sleeping, O Lord?" file_lines.section: 5. God's face hidden, as the human bears it (FH) — 31 verses
file_lines.text: - Psa 51:9 → 51:10 "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me". **New in v3:** when God is asked to hide his face *from the sin*, the next request places the remedy in **the heart and spirit**. The seat is where the cleansing is to happen. The requests go on: "Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (51:11), then "uphold me with a willing spirit" (51:12). **The face hidden from the sin (51:9) is set against the presence not withdrawn from the person (51:11).** Between them stand two spirits: God's, which is not to be taken away, and the human's, which is to be renewed and made willing.

In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

**Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

file_lines.section: 1.3 Refusing God: what was offered, and what it was refused for
file_lines.text: **Pro 1:29–31 and Psa 81:11–12 put choosing, willing and one's own counsels or devices into a single sentence.** In Proverbs: did not choose, would have none of my counsel, their own devices. In the psalm: would not submit, their stubborn hearts, their own counsels. These are the places where Scripture itself sets the acts side by side. Both say what follows: being given over to one's own counsels, and being filled with one's own devices. They do not say these acts form one sequence in every person, and these notes do not say it either.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": §2b batch 1, those who are chosen, Old Testament (2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Psa 65:4, Psa 105:43, Psa 106:5, Isa 43:10, Isa 44:2)
file_lines.text: - Psalm 105:1–45 and Psalm 106:1–48

The verse follows straight on: *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (v43). The joy and singing are set on the people brought out. They come with being brought out, and the bringing out comes from God remembering his promise. The chosen are told to remember (v5) because he remembered (v8, v42).
- joy and singing (Psa 105:43)

In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

**The return is the Lord's remembering.** He remembered his covenant at their cry (Psa 106:44–45). He remembered his promise and brought them out with joy (Psa 105:42–43). He blots out their sins and will not remember them (Isa 43:25). The chosen are called to remember in turn (Psa 105:5; Isa 44:21).
- "So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing" (Psa 105:43)

file_lines.section: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"
file_lines.text: The speaker asks to be included: *"Remember me, O Lord, when you show favor to your people; help me when you save them, that I may look upon the prosperity of your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance"* (v4–5). He does not claim the chosen ones' gladness. He asks to look upon it and to share it. "Gladness" here (H8057) is the same word as David's *"rejoicing"* in 2 Samuel 6:12.
- gladness, which another asks to share (Psa 106:5)

file_lines.section: With the chosen, and for them
file_lines.text: The chosen also stand for the others. *"Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath"* (Psa 106:23). The psalm sets these side by side and does not comment.

file_lines.section: Psalm 119:30 — "I have chosen the way of faithfulness"
file_lines.text: The false way is not refused by his own strength alone. He asks God to put it at a distance. Then he states the choice: *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (v30). The choosing is joined at once to keeping something in view: he puts the rules in front of himself, where he can see them.

file_lines.section: Making the choice, and holding it
file_lines.text: - **It is held by keeping in view and clinging.** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies"* (Psa 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used two verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). What the soul clings to has turned.

- **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).
**Envy.** The pull can be named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).

file_lines.section: 3. A husband's jealousy with no witness (10.6)
file_lines.text: Num 5:14–31. The "spirit of jealousy" comes over the husband whether the wife "has defiled herself" or "has not" (5:14): the law itself says the jealousy may be wrong. The offering is "of jealousy … of remembrance", with no oil and no frankincense (5:15). The matter is not his to settle: "he shall set the woman before the Lord" (5:30); "The man shall be free from iniquity" (5:31). Beside Pro 6:34–35, where a husband's jealousy "will accept no compensation", **I read** the law as taking the jealousy out of the husband's hands and putting it before God. Num 5:18 and 5:25 (the ritual) are carried by this account.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing as preferring.** *"to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16): to choose is to weigh and set above. What is to be preferred is inward, and it is valued above *"nothing you desire"* (Pro 3:15).

file_lines.section: Job 36:21 — Elihu: "this you have chosen rather than affliction"
file_lines.text: His evaluation: *"Take care; do not turn to iniquity, for this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (v21). The choice he sees is a preference, as in Proverbs 16:16 (*"rather than"*). Of the two things before Job, affliction (H6040, the word in v15) and iniquity (H0205), Elihu says Job has taken iniquity rather than accept the affliction as the opening of his ear. The warning *"Take care"* treats the choice as still able to be turned.

**Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good against another and set it above: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Pro 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets the weighing against all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).

- **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

file_lines.section: 10. The will invited, refused, bound and set on godliness
file_lines.text: - **Compare Isa 1:19**, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*. Both put the will before a good with an "if".

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 1 — the Isaiah oracles (Isa 1:29, Isa 66:3–4, Isa 7:15–16)
Isaiah 1:29 — "the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen"
file_lines.text: - the two outcomes: *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (v19–20)

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20).** *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

The choice is laid out with both its sides and both its ends: *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*; *"but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:16–20).

- The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"*, the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (Isa 7:15, 22). In the other oracle, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (Isa 1:19).

file_lines.section: 3. The Hebrew: the will is the yes or no to another
file_lines.text: *ʾāḇâ* (H0014) has 52 verses. **50 of them are negated**: "would not", "not willing", "unwilling", "refuse", "would have none". The other two are a question that expects "no" (*"Is the wild ox willing to serve you?"*, Job 39:9) and a condition (*"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"*, Isa 1:19).

file_lines.section: 1.3 Refusing God: what was offered, and what it was refused for
file_lines.text: - **Cleansing, after reasoning:** *"Come now, let us reason together … though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow … If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isa 1:18–20). This is the one place in the set where the will is invited with "if". Both ways are set out, as in *Life and death set before a person* (10.7).

- **F3. Isa 7:15–16 (entry 20).** The verses name a capacity to choose, not a choice made. It stays in §2a as "ground", but it is a different kind of entry from the others.

file_lines.section: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"
file_lines.text: "Despised" in v24 is H3988A, the same word as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. The chosen people refused what they were given. "Faith" in v24 is H0539, the same word as *"believed"* in v12. The psalm has them believing, then forgetting, then without faith.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 43:10: "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand"
file_lines.text: This is the reverse of the order in §2a, where the child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). There the knowing comes before the person's own choosing. Here, the knowing follows God's choosing of the person. Each verse states its own order.

**Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 7:15–16 — "when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"
file_lines.text: The sign is given anyway, and at its centre is a child who has what Ahaz lacked: *"He shall eat curds and honey when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (v15). The act is one act with two sides:

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing rests on knowing how (Isa 7:15).** It is a knowing *how* to tell evil from good and turn. In Isa 1 the oracle opens with its absence: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is laid out as an offer, with both outcomes (Isa 1:16–20).** *"cease to do evil, learn to do good"*; *"willing"* or *"refuse"*; eat, or be eaten. In Isa 7:15 the right choice also ends in eating.

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: - *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (v13). "Well-being" here (H2896B) is the same word as *"the good"* in Isaiah 7:15, *"refuse the evil and choose the good"*. The man taught the way he should choose has his soul *"abide"*, lodge or stay, in the good.

file_lines.section: Psalm 25:12 — "Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"
file_lines.text: The psalmist then turns his eyes: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord, for he will pluck my feet out of the net"* (v15). Where the eyes are turned decides where the feet are kept from.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The good chosen is the good the soul lives in.** Isaiah 7:15 has *"choose the good"*, and Psalm 25:13 has *"His soul shall abide in well-being"*. It is the same word (H2896B). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place where the soul lives. Each verse says its own half; neither refers to the other.

file_lines.section: 2 Samuel 19:38 — "whatever seems good to you, and all that you desire of me"
file_lines.text: Barzillai declines, and his reason is about his own inner capacity: *"I am this day eighty years old. Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not? Can your servant taste what he eats or what he drinks? Can I still listen to the voice of singing men and singing women?"* (v35). The Hebrew is "know between good and evil" (H3045 with H0996, H2896B, H7451A). It is the same pairing as Isaiah 7:15–16, *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"*. Here it is the knowing of taste and pleasure, and Barzillai says that at eighty it has gone. The same words, put to the palate rather than to right and wrong, mark a change of face (#1919).

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The knowing of good and evil has more than one face.** In Isa 7:15 it is the knowing that grounds choosing the good. In 2Sa 19:35 the same words are the palate's knowing of pleasant and unpleasant, and they fade with age.

file_lines.section: Job 34:33 — Elihu: "For you must choose, and not I"
file_lines.text: - **The refusing word comes back.** *"because you reject it"* uses H3988A, the same verb as *"refuse the evil"* in Isaiah 7:15. Elihu says Job is refusing, and that God will not repay on Job's terms because of it.

file_lines.section: What batch 4 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The refusing verb returns at the end.** Elihu's *"you reject"* and Job's *"I despise … and repent"* are the same verb (34:33; 42:6), the verb of *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15). In Job the choice is made when *"now my eye sees you"* (42:5). This stands beside the test reading of Jos 24, where the people chose from what they had seen.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: Scripture does not stop to define choosing. In these verses it shows choosing as an act with two sides. The clearest sentence is about a child: *"when he knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). Refusing and choosing are one act, seen from either side. The man the book of Job calls blameless is described by his refusing: he *"feared God and turned away from evil"* (Job 1:1). The father in Proverbs puts the choice entirely in the negative: *"do not choose any of his ways"* (Pro 3:31).
- *"refuse the evil"* (Isa 7:15)

Refusing is itself choosing. The child *"knows how to refuse the evil and choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle around that verse shows refusing going both ways. Ahaz refuses the Lord's offer of a sign with pious words: *"I will not ask, and I will not put the Lord to the test"* (Isa 7:12). The people *"refused the waters of Shiloah that flow gently"* (8:6). The right refusing and the wrong refusing are set in one oracle, each with its own consequence.
**Knowing how.** The child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isa 7:15). The oracle of Isaiah 1 opens with the absence of that knowing: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3).

- *"His soul shall abide in well-being"* (Psa 25:13). "Well-being" is the same word as *"the good"* in *"choose the good"* (Isa 7:15). I read this as the good that is chosen becoming the place the soul lives.

- The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"*, the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (Isa 7:15, 22). In the other oracle, *"If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land"* (Isa 1:19).
- It is the knowing that grounds the moral choice (Isa 7:15–16).
- It is refusing the evil (Isa 7:15).

file_lines.section: M64 plan set: the 77 inner-being planning verses woven (account, v1, 2026-10-08)
file_lines.text: - **How they were read:** each verse in its passage (two verses either side, more where the passage needed it), in the ESV text from iba.db. Some verses routed A and B were also used for their human side, where they belong to the same account: Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38; Gen 50:20; 1Ch 28:9; 29:18; Isa 26:3; 1Co 4:5.

| **10.7 Choosing and setting direction**, new section ***Planning*** | The account of looking ahead. Planning carries a choice ahead (Gen 11:6; Pro 16:9). It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section |

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).

file_lines.section: 4.2 God stirs the spirit: toward building, and toward destroying
file_lines.text: - **The stirred person still acts as himself.** Cyrus makes a proclamation and writes it down. The Medes *"have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold"* (Isa 13:17), and Cyrus works *"not for price or reward"* (45:13). Both stirred agents are men who cannot be bought. **I read** that God stirs a spirit already suited to the task. The verses do not say whether the stirring makes it so.

verses.text: He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.

observations.text: In Isa 40.20 'seeks out' functions within the base gloss of seeking-to-secure (a craftsman), a straightforward practical-search sense with no notable added nuance.
The impoverished man (implied party, 'he') initiates the seeking-operation, directed toward a skillful craftsman (party) to make an idol -- seeking here serves an idolatrous construction project.

M64 (chooses, wood-selection), M16 (skillful), M23/M55 (setting up an idol) are present but describe separate stages of idol-making; seeking here specifically targets the craftsman, distinct from those other characteristics' own referents.

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": §2b batch 1, those who are chosen, Old Testament (2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Psa 65:4, Psa 105:43, Psa 106:5, Isa 43:10, Isa 44:2)
file_lines.text: - Isaiah 43:1–44:28, one run of oracles
- knowing, believing and understanding (Isa 43:10)

In 2Sa 6:21, 1Ch 28:10, Isa 43:10 and Isa 44:2 the verse names the being chosen as the ground or the reason. In Psa 65:4 the response follows the choosing in the same sentence. In Psa 105:43 and 106:5, "chosen ones" names the people whose joy it is; the verse does not make the choosing the cause.

**Being chosen comes before the inner act, not after it.** In §2a, knowing, fear and teaching came before a person's own choosing (Isa 7:15; Psa 25:12). In Isaiah 43:10, God chooses first, and knowing is the purpose. The chosen were blind and deaf when chosen (43:8). In Psalm 65 they were chosen after their iniquity was atoned for (v3–4).

**For batch 2:** the 8 New Testament verses. In five of them (Eph 1:4, 2Th 2:13, Tit 1:1, Jam 2:5, 2Pe 1:10) the inner act is given as the purpose of the choosing, or as the call that follows it. Whether they keep the order seen in Isaiah 43:10, with the choosing first and the knowing after, is to be read from them.
**The order seen in Isaiah 43:10 holds, and is widened.** God chooses first, and the inner life of the chosen is the purpose:
- the purpose of being chosen: Isa 43:10
- "my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (Isa 43:10)

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

file_lines.section: Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing
file_lines.text: **Not knowing, and still used.** Cyrus is called for the sake of the chosen: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isa 45:4). And *"I equip you, though you do not know me"* (45:5). Knowing is held out as the purpose: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3).
- Not knowing God does not stop a man from being called for the sake of the chosen (Isa 45:4–5).

file_lines.section: Psalm 106:5: "that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance"
file_lines.text: He asks it while confessing: *"Both we and our fathers have sinned; we have committed iniquity; we have done wickedness"* (v6). The rest of the psalm shows what the chosen people did (v7–43).
- despise and abhor the chosen servant (Isa 49:7)

**Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").

**What God does in reply.** In Num 17:5 he makes the choice plain. In Isa 49:7 he promises that kings will bow. In Jer 33:25–26 he points to the fixed order of day and night. Under rule 72 these acts are God's and go to Ch 13. They are recorded here because each one answers what the others did.

**The same word in two verses.** Michal's *"despised"* (2Sa 6:16) and the servant *"deeply despised"* (Isa 49:7) are the same verb, *bāzâ* (H0959). The verses are side by side. The text does not join them.

file_lines.section: Others around a choice, in the human inner being — the account from the §2c readings
file_lines.text: **Scope:** The account covers people who stand near a choice someone else made: at what was chosen, turned toward it, set against it, standing with the chosen, or knowing of the choice. In all but one of the readings the chooser is God. In 1Sa 20:30 it is Jonathan. God's own acts in reply (Num 17:5; Isa 45:4–5; 49:7; Jer 33:25–26; Rom 11:8; 1Pe 2:8) belong to 13.1 under rule 72. They are named here only where they answer what the others did. Readings beyond what a verse says are marked "I read".

**Despising and abhorring.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isa 49:7). "Despised" is the same verb as Michal's. The verse turns it round by God's faithfulness and choosing: *"Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*.
- The servant is *"deeply despised"* by others, and kings will bow (Isa 49:7). Same verb, *bāzâ*.

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing what the Lord delights in (Isa 56:4).** This is the counterpart to Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4. With the three verses together, "the things that please me" and "what I did not delight in" are the two sides of one measure.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The choice is held, not just made.** It is set between keeping and holding fast (Isa 56:2, 4, 6), and between eyes turned to the Lord and waiting (Psa 25:15, 21). This sits with the test readings: the heart inclined after the choice (Jos 24:23), and clinging to the testimonies (Psa 119:31).

file_lines.section: An inner act weighed by what God chooses
file_lines.text: In one passage the inner act of the others is itself set against God's choosing. The people fast and ask, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"* (Isa 58:3). They *"delight to know my ways"* and *"delight to draw near to God"* (58:2). Yet *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (58:3). Then: *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). "Humble himself" is the humbling of the soul, the same words as their own complaint. What God does choose is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7).

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Refusing is choosing (Isa 7:15–16).** The act is one act with two sides, and refusing can go either way. The child refuses the evil. Ahaz refuses the sign, and the people refuse the gentle waters (8:6), with the same verb. This sharpens the test reading of Isa 65:12, which said that not answering and not listening are already choosing: in Isa 8:6 the refusal is named outright.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: Then he describes the eunuchs he means: *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (v4). The word "please" is H2654A, the same word as *"delight"* in Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4 (*"chose what I did not delight in"*, *"chose that in which I did not delight"*). Here the choosing goes the other way. These choose what the Lord delights in. The measure is the same as in those two oracles, the Lord's delight, and here it is met.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: - Choosing what the Lord delights in is the positive counterpart to choosing what he does not delight in (65:12, 66:4). The measure is the same.

file_lines.section: What batch 2 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing what the Lord delights in (Isa 56:4).** This is the counterpart to Isaiah 65:12 and 66:4. With the three verses together, "the things that please me" and "what I did not delight in" are the two sides of one measure.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in"
file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 65:12 — "chose what I did not delight in"
file_lines.text: The answer turns on their own word: *"I will destine you to the sword"* (v12). In Hebrew, "Destiny" (Meni, H4507) and "destine" (manah, H4487) come from the same root. They poured cups for Destiny, and the Lord destines them. What they chose to trust becomes the form their judgement takes.
- **"In whose eyes":** Jos 24:15 has *"evil in your eyes"*, and Isa 65:12 has *"evil in my eyes"*.

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [the test](m64-choose-test-reading-v1-20261007.md): Jos 24:15, Psa 119:30, Isa 65:12

Not answering is already choosing. *"when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12; repeated in 66:4). The choosing of what the Lord does not delight in is where the not-listening ends up.
- **The Lord's eyes.** *"you did what was evil in my eyes"* (Isa 65:12). The measure is the Lord's sight.
- **The Lord's delight, failed.** *"chose what I did not delight in"* (Isa 65:12); *"chose that in which I did not delight"* (66:4).
- They set *"cups of mixed wine for Destiny"*, and the Lord says *"I will destine you to the sword"*. "Destiny" and "destine" share a root (Isa 65:11–12).
- It gives way to *"evil in my eyes"*, the Lord's sight (Isa 65:12).

- **Delight (H2654A).** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isa 66:3). It is the Lord's delight as the measure, either failed (Isa 65:12; 66:4) or met (Isa 56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.

file_lines.text: ## Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: Against that stands worship that looks right and is not: *"He who slaughters an ox is like one who kills a man; he who sacrifices a lamb, like one who breaks a dog’s neck"* … *"like one who blesses an idol"* (v3). The outward act is the same as before; what has gone wrong is inside. The verse says where: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations."* Choosing and the soul’s delight stand side by side. They chose their own ways, and their soul (H5315) takes pleasure in what the Lord calls abominations.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: - their soul *"delights"* in abominations (v3)

file_lines.section: What batch 1 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Choosing goes with desire and delight.** It is paired with *"desired"* (1:29) and with the soul’s delight (66:3). In Isa 66 the delight word is the same on both sides, so the choice is a question of whose delight governs it.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 56:4 — "who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"
file_lines.text: What follows in the chapter is the opposite. Israel's own watchmen *"are all without knowledge"*. They are *"shepherds who have no understanding; they have all turned to their own way, each to his own gain"* (v10–11). "Their own way" is the same phrase as in Isaiah 66:3, *"These have chosen their own ways"* (H1870G). The outsiders who choose what the Lord delights in are brought in. The insiders turn to their own way.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **The pull before the choice.** *"Do not envy … and do not choose"* (Pro 3:31): the command reaches the envy as well as the choice. This stands beside batch 1, where *"desired"* is paired with *"chosen"* (Isa 1:29) and the soul's delight with choosing one's own ways (Isa 66:3).

file_lines.section: Choosing in the human inner being — the account from the §2a readings
file_lines.text: - [batch 1](m64-choose-reading-batch1-isaiah-v1-20261007.md): Isa 1:29, Isa 66:3, Isa 7:15–16

**Desire and delight.** Choosing comes paired with desire: *"the oaks that you desired … the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isa 1:29). It comes with the soul's delight: *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3).
- **The soul's own delight, set against the Lord's.** *"their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isa 66:3). The word is the same one again.

- **The choosing verb (H0977).** It is used for choosing a master (Jos 24:15), a place (Deu 23:16), a way (Psa 119:30; Isa 66:3), a preference (Pro 16:16), and a verdict (Job 34:4). *Why:* it is turned to whatever is set before a person.

- **Delight (H2654A).** It is the soul's own delight in what it chose (Isa 66:3). It is the Lord's delight as the measure, either failed (Isa 65:12; 66:4) or met (Isa 56:4). *Why:* whose delight it is decides.
