file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: The Lord’s answer is a choice of his own, in the same verb: *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (v4). What he brings is *their fears* (H4035): what they themselves dreaded. Set against v2 and v5, the contrast is in the inner being. The one who *"trembles at my word"* is looked on. Those who chose their own ways are given what they feared.

file_lines.section: Isaiah 66:3–4 — "These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"
file_lines.text: The reason is given in the same words as 65:12: *"because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen; but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight"* (v4). Their choosing is the end of not answering and not listening.

file_lines.section: 1.4 He also purposes and does not turn back
file_lines.text: **Both are stated.** The verses say he relents (Jer 18:8, 10; 26:3; 36:3) and that he does not relent or turn back (Jer 4:28; Zec 8:14; Heb 6:17). No verse in this set explains how the two stand together, and this account does not.

file_lines.text: - **Turning:** in Jer 18:8, 11; 26:3 and 36:3, the plan is spoken so that a person may hear and turn.
| H2803I | God shaping disaster that he may relent from (Jer 18:8, 11); God's plans for welfare (Jer 29:11); people devising evil (Psa 35:4); Saul's plot (1Sa 18:25); a ship "threatened" (Jon 1:4) |

**God's intentions in Jeremiah are conditional:** *"if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended"* (Jer 18:8; also 26:3, 36:3). His plan is stated so that people may *"Return, every one from his evil way"* (Jer 18:11). file_lines.text: - Jeremiah 33:19–26
- conclude from the chosen people's ruin that God rejected them, and despise them in their own sight (Jer 33:24)

**Whose measure.** It comes up in four verses. Michal measures by *"the eyes of his servants' female servants"* (2Sa 6:20). The people in Jer 33:24 measure *"in their sight"*. Over against both, David celebrates *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:21), and Isa 49:7 gives the Lord's faithfulness and choosing. The same theme is in batch 1 (Deu 12:8) and in §2a ("whose measure").
**Whose measure.** *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4). This sits with batch 1 (Deu 12:8), batch 2 (2Sa 6:20; Jer 33:24) and §2a.

file_lines.text: - [batch 2](m64-choose-2c-reading-batch2-others-ot-v1-20261008.md), other Old Testament: Num 17:5, Judg 20:34, 1Sa 20:30, 2Sa 6:16, Psa 106:5, Psa 106:23, Pro 10:20, Isa 7:16, Isa 45:4, Isa 49:7, Isa 58:5, Isa 66:3, Jer 33:24

**A conclusion drawn from ruin.** *"'The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose'? Thus they have despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jer 33:24). Others look at the state of the chosen, decide God has rejected them, and despise them on that ground. God's answer is that his choosing is as fixed as day and night (33:25–26).

**Whose eyes.** In four of these the measure is named, and it is set against God's: *"in his own eyes"* against the place God chooses (Deu 12:8); *"before the eyes of his servants' female servants"* against *"before the Lord"* (2Sa 6:20–21); *"in their sight"* (Jer 33:24); *"rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen"* (1Pe 2:4).
- Others *"despised my people"*, concluding that God had rejected them (Jer 33:24; *nāʾaṣ*).

verses.text: For any one of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn in Israel, who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart and putting the stumbling block of his iniquity before his face, and yet comes to a prophet to consult me through him, I the Lord will answer him myself.

observations.text: In Ezek.14.7 'consult' carries the nuance of hypocritical or corrupted inquiry -- the idolater comes to a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart; the impact is that the surface act of seeking is emptied of sincerity, contrasting sharply with the sincere seeking of Isa.55.6 and 2Chr.1.5.

Other M-codes in Ezek.14.7 (M01 sojourn, M64 separates, M47 heart, M15 putting, M77 stumbling block, M56 iniquity, M43 prophet, M22 answer) surround the consulting act but are not positively related to it: darash here is corrupted by co-present idolatry (M77/M56) rather than harmonizing with them -- the seeking is nullified by what accompanies it, a distinct vantage from any prior finding.

In Ezek.14.7, H1875 is the role-T3 operation: the idolater ('any one', party) initiates consulting, directed toward God via a prophet (parties), though the act is compromised by the idolater's simultaneous devotion to idols.

Isa.31.1 and Ezek.14.7 both use 'consult' of illegitimate or compromised inquiry -- Isa.31.1 negates true consultation of the Lord in favor of trust in horses/chariots, while Ezek.14.7 depicts an idolater hypocritically approaching a prophet to consult God while harboring idols in his heart. Both instances show darash's consultation-sense corrupted or withheld by competing loyalties.

Seeking takes hold rightly under conditions of wholeheartedness and sincerity: 'set your mind and heart to seek' (1Chr.22.19), 'with all their heart and with all their soul' (2Chr.15.12), and freedom from co-present idolatry -- in Ezek.14.7 the presence of idols in the heart is what disqualifies otherwise-outward consultation. Genuine seeking requires an undivided heart free from rival objects of devotion.

Seeking is blocked or nullified when the heart harbors idols or a stumbling block of iniquity even while outwardly consulting God -- Ezek.14.3, 14.7 explicitly describe men who 'have taken their idols into their hearts' yet 'come to a prophet to consult me' -- God declares he will not let himself be consulted (or will answer in judgment) in such cases; similarly pride (Ps.10.4 'in the pride of his face') suppresses seeking altogether.

The person whose outward act of inquiry does not take hold rightly is inwardly divided: Ezek.14.3-7 describes them as having 'taken their idols into their hearts' and 'put the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- the inner-being state is one of divided loyalty and self-deception, performing the religious gesture of consultation while the heart remains given to a rival object of devotion.

Uptake of a sought answer from another (a prophet, an oracle) is blocked when the inquirer's heart harbors rival loyalties -- Ezek.14.3-7 shows that idols hidden in the heart nullify the legitimacy of the consultation even though the outward act of inquiry is performed; genuine uptake requires the wholehearted disposition seen elsewhere (2Chr.15.12).

The person who inquires but does not genuinely take up what is sought (as in Ezek.14.3-7) is inwardly divided, harboring 'idols... into their heart' and 'the stumbling block of their iniquity before their face' -- an inner-being state of duplicity, where the outward gesture of consultation masks an unyielded heart.

The pattern of engagement shows heart/soul faculties (mind, will, affection) consistently engaged when seeking is genuine (1Chr.22.19 'set your mind and heart', 2Chr.15.12 'with all their heart and with all their soul'), while purely external/ritual engagement without heart involvement is exposed as illegitimate (Ezek.14.3-7) -- indicating the characteristic's nature is fundamentally a volitional-relational act requiring the engagement of the inner faculties, not a mechanical or merely verbal performance.

At its edge, seeking excludes casual, passive, or half-hearted attention -- it resists mere outward performance without inner devotion (Ezek.14.3-7's idol-hearted consulters are the negative exemplar), and it excludes self-sufficiency/pride that renders inquiry unnecessary (Ps.10.4).

observations.text: Fear of a people or a person falls on others. "many from the peoples of the country declared themselves Jews, for fear of the Jews had fallen on them"; officials "helped the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them". Of Nebuchadnezzar: "because of the greatness that he gave him, all peoples, nations, and languages trembled and feared before him. Whom he would, he killed". Of Ephraim: "When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died". Of the king of Babylon: "Is this the man who made the earth tremble"

Meaning: dread is laid by God, or falls because of his people, and the verses say what it did: the cities did not pursue. Implies: in Rahab, the dread came by hearing, melted heart and spirit, and ends in a confession of God. In Moab, the same dread ends in hiring a curse. Psa 9:20 asks for fear so that the nations know what they are.

verses.text: Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand.

observations.text: The bed hosts both deliberate plotting and meditation on God. The same place carries opposite directions
The path: arising → lodging → reckoning → devising → expression (tongue, lips, eyes) → action (hand, feet)

Flow 5: what is devised comes back. The plan returns on the deviser's head (Est 9:25); the schemer is caught in his own scheme (Psa 10:2); disaster is "the fruit of their devices" (Jer 6:19). God answers "devise wickedness" with "I am devising disaster" (Mic 2:1, 3). It also comes back for good: "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Pro 21:5); "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3)

file_lines.section: 1.4 He also purposes and does not turn back
file_lines.text: **Both are stated.** The verses say he relents (Jer 18:8, 10; 26:3; 36:3) and that he does not relent or turn back (Jer 4:28; Zec 8:14; Heb 6:17). No verse in this set explains how the two stand together, and this account does not.

file_lines.section: 2. Where these verses touch the human inner being (route A and B)
file_lines.text: - **Fear not:** *"so again have I purposed … to bring good … fear not"* (Zec 8:15), with commands that follow (8:16–17), including *"do not devise evil in your hearts against one another"*. The verb is the one used for his own purposing in 8:14–15.

file_lines.section: 4. Where the surface varies within one Strong's
file_lines.text: - **G1165 *deigmatizō*:** Joseph "unwilling to put her to shame" (Mat 1:19) beside Christ who "put them to open shame" (Col 2:15).

file_lines.section: 6. Other M-codes in the same verses
file_lines.text: - **M18 (20 shared verses).** Read or decided in the M18 strand (for example Luk 18:4 carried in 10.12, Mat 1:19 in 10.7 *Willing*, 1Co 14:35 data). None was forwarded to M07.

file_lines.section: 6. Other M-codes in the same verses
file_lines.text: - **There is no section on shame.** The one section with shame in its heading is **10.3 *Remembering in shame*** (Eze 16:63; 20:43). Shame otherwise appears in passing: 10.7 *Shame at the thing chosen* (Isa 1:29; 65:13), Saul's "to your own shame" (1Sa 20:30) in 10.7, Joseph "unwilling to put her to shame" (Mat 1:19) in 10.7, Ephraim "ashamed and confounded" (Jer 31:19) in 13.1, "some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Dan 12:2) in Ch 2, and *In shame* (Php 3:19) in 10.15.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: - **A resolve reached after weighing, then turned.** *"her husband Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly"* (Mat 1:19). The next verse: *"But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (1:20). The resolve was still being weighed, and God redirected it.

file_lines.section: 1.6 The will that resolves, intends and steers
file_lines.text: - **Joseph.** *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Mat 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, he resolved, and he went on considering. Then God spoke into the considering.

file_lines.section: 2.2 Passages where Scripture itself puts them together
file_lines.text: 7. **Mat 1:19–20.** Unwilling, then resolved, while still considering, then redirected by God.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: All four have the step gloss "plan". One word, G1013, is rendered "plan" in one verse and "will" in another. And G1014 is rendered "chooses": *"anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22). In Greek, then, willing, choosing and planning are spoken of with one family of words. This is a fact about the words. What it means for the inner being is still to be read verse by verse.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: All four have the step gloss "plan". One word, G1013, is rendered "plan" in one verse and "will" in another. And G1014 is rendered "chooses": *"anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22). In Greek, then, willing, choosing and planning are spoken of with one family of words. This is a fact about the words. What it means for the inner being is still to be read verse by verse.

2. **Route them under rule 72.** By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).

- **The Son chooses:** *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Mat 11:26–27; Luk 10:21–22). The Father's gracious will and the Son's choosing stand together. Luke adds *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (10:21).

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: **And at Gethsemane:** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done"* (Luk 22:42). This is the one verse in the set where two wills are named side by side and one is given up to the other.

2. **Route them under rule 72.** By scan, God's or the Spirit's will (route A) is 21 verses: Deu 10:10; 23:5; 29:20; Jos 24:10; 2Ki 8:19; 13:23; 24:4; 2Ch 21:7; Dan 4:17, 25, 32, 35; 5:21; Mat 11:27; Luk 10:22; Luk 22:42 (with B); Rom 9:19; 1Co 12:11; Heb 6:17; Jam 1:18; 2Pe 3:9. Job 39:9 is the wild ox (13.4 Nature).

- **Gethsemane (A and B):** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luk 22:42–44). Before it: *"Pray that you may not enter into temptation"* (22:40).

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).
- **Also B:** Deu 10:10 (Moses' intercession), Deu 29:20 (the self-blessing heart), Dan 4:25 and 4:32 (the king's learning), Dan 5:21, Luk 22:42.

It covers: weighing first (Luk 14:28–33; Pro 31:15–16; Judg 19:30); planning without knowing (Act 27:10–14, 39–41; Rom 1:13; Jam 4:15); a plan carrying a person's word (2Co 1:17–18); planning together and parting (Act 15:37–39; Luk 23:51–52); planning for another's good (Dan 6:3–4), with the king's planning measured against God's (2Sa 14:13–14); a purpose held (Psa 17:3, 5; Act 11:23; 2Ti 3:10; 1Ch 29:18; Rom 8:6–7; Isa 26:3); devised from one's own heart (1Ki 12:32–33; Neh 6:8); the plan and its outcome (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38–39; Psa 21:11; Dan 11:24; Gen 50:20); seen and disclosed (1Ch 28:9; 1Co 4:3–5) | New section |

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).

file_lines.text: - Willing: pressing (Judg 19:7–9; 2Sa 13:25–27), enticing (Deu 13:6–8; Pro 1:10), the crowd (Mar 15:15), friends restraining or encouraging (Act 19:30–31; 18:27), objection (Act 28:19), consent sought so that the good is free (Phm 14).

file_lines.section: 2.3 The same thing showing in both readings
file_lines.text: - **The outcome is not held.** Plans fail or are overruled (Pro 16:9; Isa 8:10; Act 5:38). Wills are overruled as well: Herod's intention (Act 12), the Romans' wish to free Paul (Act 28:18–19), Paul's wish to enter the theater (Act 19:30). And human will is set under God's: *"it depends not on human will or exertion"* (Rom 9:16); *"not my will, but yours"* (Luk 22:42).

file_lines.text: - **What it is.** Knowing that cannot close: a mind held open before something it cannot interpret. - **Who bears it:** Herod (Mar 6:20; Luk 9:7); the disciples (Joh 13:22); the women at the tomb (Luk 24:4); the Pentecost crowd (Act 2:12); the temple captain and chief priests (Act 5:24); Peter (Act 10:17); Festus (Act 25:20); Paul (2Cor 4:8; Gal 4:20); Belshazzar's lords (Dan 5:9).

- **What it does.** It **asks aloud**: "What does this mean?" (Act 2:12); "who is this about whom I hear such things?" (Luk 9:9). It **looks at others**: "The disciples looked at one another" (Joh 13:22). It **turns inward**: "Peter was inwardly [*en heautō*, in himself] perplexed" (Act 10:17). Festus **hands the question on**: "Being at a loss how to investigate … I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem" (Act 25:20).

file_lines.section: M64 "choose": batch 3 — choosing of one's own accord, choosing together, and the wisdom sayings
2 Corinthians 8:17 — "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"
file_lines.text: The chapter is about giving to the poor saints. It opens with the Macedonians: *"in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity"* (v2). They gave *"according to their means … and beyond their means, of their own accord"* (v3). That is the same word as in v17 (G0830, *authairetos*, "self-chosen"). The order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (v5). Their own accord and the will of God stand side by side in one sentence.

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Own accord alongside God's working.** Titus goes *"of his own accord"* after God *"put into the heart"* the care (2Cor 8:16–17). The Macedonians give *"of their own accord"*, having given themselves to the Lord *"by the will of God"* (8:3, 5). Both are named and neither cancels the other. This sits with batch 2 (the way to choose is taught) and the test (Psa 119:32, the heart enlarged by God).
- "they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord" (2Cor 8:3)
- **G0830, "of one's own accord".** One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

file_lines.section: Own accord, and God at work
file_lines.text: The Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and the order of their giving is set out: *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5). The church's choice is joined to the Spirit's in the same verb: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Act 15:28). The psalmist chooses, and asks God to give the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psa 119:32). I read these verses as saying that what God puts into the heart becomes the person's own. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.

file_lines.text: Titus is described the same way: *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (v16–17). The verse holds three things together:

file_lines.section: What batch 3 adds to the account of choosing
file_lines.text: - **Own accord alongside God's working.** Titus goes *"of his own accord"* after God *"put into the heart"* the care (2Cor 8:16–17). The Macedonians give *"of their own accord"*, having given themselves to the Lord *"by the will of God"* (8:3, 5). Both are named and neither cancels the other. This sits with batch 2 (the way to choose is taught) and the test (Psa 119:32, the heart enlarged by God).
- "being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord" (2Cor 8:17)

file_lines.text: - [batch 3](m64-choose-reading-batch3-own-accord-together-v1-20261007.md): Deu 23:16, 2Sa 19:38, 2Cor 8:17, Act 6:5, Act 15:22 and 25, Pro 3:31, Pro 16:16
- **G0830, "of one's own accord".** One word, literally "self-chosen" (2Cor 8:3, 17).

**Being pleased, and earnestness.** In the church at Jerusalem the choosing comes out of a shared inward response: *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose"* (Act 6:5). Titus goes *"being himself very earnest … of his own accord"* (2Cor 8:17).

verses.text: But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth.

observations.text: In 2Thess.2.13 'we ought always to give thanks to God for you' diverges from the meal-blessing sense dominant in the Gospels/Acts/1Cor occurrences of this cluster -- here thanksgiving is a sustained, obligatory disposition ('ought always') directed at other believers' salvation-status (election, sanctification, belief) rather than a single ritual act over food. The impact is to broaden eucharisteo from a punctual liturgical gesture to an ongoing pastoral duty of gratitude for others' spiritual condition.

In 2Thess.2.13, thanksgiving (G2168) co-occurs with M14 (brothers), M51 (beloved), M64 (chose), M16 (firstfruits), M79 (saved), M61 (sanctification), M13 (belief/truth, twice). Thanksgiving is the responsive frame surrounding this entire chain: it is offered specifically because of God's prior acts of choosing, sanctifying, and saving -- thanksgiving here functions as the grateful acknowledgment of the whole soteriological sequence rather than being caused by any single other M-code term alone.

In 2Thess.2.13, arche appears in the specialized sense 'firstfruits' rather than its more common gloss 'beginning/rule/authority' -- a divergence that carries covenantal-agricultural nuance (a consecrated, representative first portion) distinct from the term's dominant temporal or governmental senses elsewhere in the NT.
In 2Thess.2.13 'brothers' sits within the base NT sense of fellow believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'beloved by the Lord' sits within the base NT sense of God's settled love for believers; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'chose' sits within the base sense of God's electing choice; no notable divergence.
In 2Thess.2.13 'saved' sits within the base theological sense of eschatological salvation; no notable divergence.

In 2Thess.2.13 the sense shifts from a single concrete act (over food) to an ongoing obligation ('ought always to give thanks'), infinitive form, directed not at provision of a meal but at God's whole saving work (chosen, sanctified, saved) -- the nuance here is thanksgiving as continuous doxological duty rather than a discrete ritual moment, contrasting with the meal-occurrences.

Adding to the prior finding for 2Thess.2.13: from thanksgiving's own vantage, it functions specifically as an obligatory (opheilomen, 'we ought') response, distinguishing it from the other M-codes present (chosen M64, sanctification M61, belief/truth M13) which describe what God has done TO the believers, while thanksgiving alone names the believers' required responsive posture toward that whole complex.
In 2Thess.2.13 Paul and companions ('we', party) initiate the thanksgiving operation, directed toward God (party), on behalf of the Thessalonian brothers (party) for God's saving work toward them.

The large majority of G2168's occurrences (Rom.1.8; 1Cor.1.4; Eph.5.20; Col.1.3; 1Thess.5.18; Rev.11.17; 2Thess.2.13; Rom.16.4; 1Thess.2.13; 2Thess.1.3; 1Cor.1.14; 1Cor.14.18; Phil.1.3; 1Thess.1.2; Phlm.1.4; 1Cor.10.30; Col.1.12; 2Cor.1.11; Eph.1.16) share one core sense across the strong's own full occurrence list: an epistolary/liturgical, habitual first- or plural-person verb of thanking God, usually 'always'/'constantly' and grounded in some grace, faith, or benefit already received in the addressees or the speaker. This is the dominant register of the strong internally and forms the baseline against which the meal-blessing and single exceptional uses (below) stand out.

Thanksgiving is produced by prior reception of grace (M50, 1Cor.1.4), by observing another's faith or love (M13/M51, Rom.1.8, 2Thess.1.3), and by God's qualifying/electing/saving action (M64/M61/M79, Col.1.12, 2Thess.2.13) -- it is consistently downstream of these other characteristics/divine acts.

file_lines.section: 1. What I set aside, and should not have
file_lines.text: - *dialogismos* is both inner reasoning and outward quarrel or dispute (1Ti 2:8; Php 2:14).

**4. One word covers both inner reasoning and outward dispute.** *Dialogismos* is rendered "thoughts" (Mark 7:21), but also "quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8), "disputing" (Philippians 2:14) and "opinions" (Romans 14:1). The same activity happens inside a person as an inner conversation and between people as argument.

file_lines.text: **Verses:** Mat 19:17–22; Joh 5:40 (with 5:42–44); Rut 3:13 (with 4:4–6); 2Ti 3:12. Compared with Isa 1:19 and 1Ti 6:9 (in 10.7).

file_lines.section: H. The perish words (added in v3)
file_lines.text: 5. **Stated causes of perishing.** Forgetting God and serving other gods (Deu 8:19–20; 30:18; Jos 23:16); not repenting (Luk 13:3, 5); not believing (Jude 5); desires to be rich (1Ti 6:9); "those who are far from you shall perish" (Psa 73:27); taking the sword (Mat 26:52); false witness (Pro 19:9; 21:28). Luk 13:3 and 2Th 2:10 are woven. The rest are carried by the death-in-the-living causes and stay here as sources for when those strands are read.

file_lines.section: 2. The Greek: will and plan are one family
file_lines.text: - **A will turned toward ruin.** *"those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare"* (1Ti 6:9). *"whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God"* (Jam 4:4).

- **Toward riches:** *"those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare, into many senseless and harmful desires that plunge people into ruin"* (1Ti 6:9). Beside it: *"godliness with contentment is great gain"* (6:6), and *"flee these things. Pursue righteousness"* (6:11).

file_lines.section: 1.4 He also purposes and does not turn back
file_lines.text: **Both are stated.** The verses say he relents (Jer 18:8, 10; 26:3; 36:3) and that he does not relent or turn back (Jer 4:28; Zec 8:14; Heb 6:17). No verse in this set explains how the two stand together, and this account does not.
- **Overlap with the other sets:** Heb 6:17 is also in the will set and Rom 9:11 is also in the choose set. Every other verse is new to this strand.

file_lines.section: Acts 15:7: "you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"
file_lines.text: The debate ends: *"And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened"* (v12). The assembly's own choosing follows later in the chapter: *"it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men"* (v25). That was read for §2a.

file_lines.section: Romans 11:7: "Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"
file_lines.text: Paul does not leave it there: *"So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous"* (v11). He goes on: *"how much more will their full inclusion mean!"* (v12).

file_lines.section: 2 Timothy 2:10: "Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect"
file_lines.text: "Endure" is *hupomenō* (G5278). The same word comes in the saying that follows: *"if we endure, we will also reign with him"* (v12). The endurance is Paul's. It is for others, the elect, and for their salvation.

file_lines.section: 2 Timothy 2:10: "Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect"

file_lines.section: H. The perish words (added in v3)
file_lines.text: 5. **Stated causes of perishing.** Forgetting God and serving other gods (Deu 8:19–20; 30:18; Jos 23:16); not repenting (Luk 13:3, 5); not believing (Jude 5); desires to be rich (1Ti 6:9); "those who are far from you shall perish" (Psa 73:27); taking the sword (Mat 26:52); false witness (Pro 19:9; 21:28). file_lines.text: **The epistle openings and requests** (*"I want you to know"*, Phi 1:12; Tit 3:8; Jude 5; 1Ti 2:8; 5:14; 2Jo 12; Phm 13; 3Jo 10) mostly use the word as a stated wish in teaching. Their bearing on setting direction is slight, but each still needs to be read.
